idiom_name: NullLogger.Instance / NullLogger<T>.Instance with nullable reference types
implementation_notes: The .NET ecosystem ships the pattern for its most pervasive optional dependency: NullLogger.Instance and NullLogger<T>.Instance (package Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions) are shared, sealed, no-op ILogger implementations designed to be the constructor fallback (logger ?? NullLogger<T>.Instance), so library code logs unconditionally. For a domain interface the same shape is hand-written in a few lines as a sealed class plus a shared static readonly instance, and C# 8 nullable reference types supply the complement: declare the parameter ILogger<T>? but keep the field non-nullable, so the compiler enforces that the null object - never a null reference - was substituted. Use ?. / ?? and a nullable field instead when the caller must act on absence.
pitfalls: Use 'logger ?? NullLogger.Instance' in the constructor body, not '= NullLogger.Instance' as a default parameter value: a default parameter is baked into the caller's assembly and cannot be replaced later without recompiling callers.

With nullable reference types enabled the field must stay non-nullable - otherwise the compiler stops enforcing exactly the invariant the null object exists to provide, and every '!' or '?.' in the call path is the smell that a real null can still escape.
NullLogger (non-generic) does not implement ILogger<T>; a generic dependency needs NullLogger<T>.Instance, and NullLogger<T>.Instance is the shared instance to use rather than newing one per object.
